title: Marcia's long grief
hookLine: Seneca writes to a mother still grieving her son after three years (Consolation to Marcia 1)

cards: There's a point after a death when people stop asking. The casseroles stop. The cards stop.
Everyone else's calendar has moved on, and the person who lost someone is still standing in the same room. In Rome, a woman named Marcia had reached that point.
Her son Metilius had died, and three years later, Seneca says, her grief was as fresh as the first day. So he wrote her a long letter.

teach.b: First, who she was. Marcia's father was the historian Cremutius Cordus.
Under the emperor Tiberius he was prosecuted over his history, which praised Brutus and Cassius, and he ended his own life rather than wait for the verdict. His books were ordered burned.
Marcia helped save copies, and they came back into circulation. Seneca opens the letter by honoring that courage. He doesn't start by scolding.
Second, he waited. He wouldn't have dared to argue with her grief in its first raw days, he says. He waited for time, the natural remedy, to do its work.
What worried him, three years on, was that it hadn't: grief had become a habit, feeding itself, keeping her from life. Third, two mothers.

Octavia, the sister of Augustus, lost her son Marcellus and grieved for the rest of her life. She wouldn't let anyone say his name. Livia, the wife of Augustus, lost her son Drusus and mourned him deeply.
Then she let his name back into her life, and spoke of him often, gladly. Seneca asks Marcia which she wants to be like. His test isn't whether you still miss someone.

teach.h: CAN YOU BEAR TO HEAR THE NAME?
teach.b: It's whether you can bear to hear their name. Fourth, honesty about the letter. Some readers find parts of it too quick to argue with tears, and some parents who've lost a child would say some grief never fully leaves.
Seneca's own letter shows something gentler, though.
He let her grief have its time before he said a word.

how: Some readers of Seneca's consolations make a point of speaking the name of the person who died, long after others have stopped asking.

o: a letter written to comfort someone
good luck that comes after a hard time
mourning: grief for someone who has died

games.q: Marcia's long grief — tap the pairs.
p: wouldn't let anyone say his name
spoke of her son often, gladly
how long her grief had lasted

s: Seneca wrote to Marcia in the first week after her son died
he wrote three years later, and says he wouldn't have dared argue with her grief at first.
Marcia helped save her father's books after they were ordered burned
Seneca opens the letter by honoring that courage.
Seneca holds up Octavia's lifelong grief as the model
he contrasts her with Livia, who let her son's name back into her life.

games.q: you're Livia. your son Drusus has died, and people are afraid to mention him around you. what do you do?
o: forbid anyone to speak his name.
mourn him, then let people speak of him, and speak of him yourself.
games.why: Seneca says Livia mourned deeply, then spoke of Drusus often and gladly. Octavia, grieving Marcellus, would not let his name be said.

practice: Think of someone whose loss is older than most people's patience: a friend whose parent died years ago, a neighbor whose husband is gone, maybe you.
Don't try to fix anything; just sit with them in your mind for a while, and quietly say the name of the person they lost.

wordCard.voice: Luctus. Latin for mourning: Seneca wrote to a mother three years after her son died, and asked whether she could let his name back into her life. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: mourning, the outward grief Seneca writes to Marcia about.

carryVoice: Your line: grief takes time. A name, said gently, can still be a gift. Day five hundred fourteen.
